Small charters, business jets, and a plane finder that ranks the whole year

September 16, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

Three more from the Discord thread on the new charter board.

  • Charter work for small airlines. From Matvocaat: “I like to grow my airline organically, start out small and buy the big airliners later. So charter contracts for 1–20 people would be great”. Every contract on the board asked for ninety seats or more, so a startup with two Caravans opened the page to a wall of work it could not touch. There is now a Small group charter — four to nineteen people, a wedding party or a mine crew, any aircraft that seats them — priced against the cheapest commuter aircraft that could fly it. And the board now reads your fleet: brokers post work to carriers that can fly it, so a two-Caravan outfit sees small jobs on about half its slots and a 787 operator almost never does. The big contracts do not vanish for the small carrier — there is always something to grow into — they just stop being most of the page.
  • Four business jets, and executive charters to fly them on. Also Matvocaat: “maybe you could add a few bizjets to the game? Like a CJ4 or Challenger?”. The Citation CJ4, Phenom 300E, Challenger 350 and Gulfstream G650ER are in the market. None of them will ever pay on a scheduled route — ten seats on a jet engine is the worst per-seat fuel figure in the game — and that is the point: they exist for the new Executive charter, a private party who will fly on a business jet and nothing else. Those contracts are priced against a business jet, with the cost of the aeroplane itself built into the fee the way real executive charter is priced by the hour, so a light jet kept busy on them roughly covers its lease and its margin, and a light jet sitting idle costs you exactly what it looks like. A Caravan seats the party and reaches the field; the customer still says no.
  • “Best aircraft for this route” can rank by the whole year. From ASAS: “i like the new route planner’s plane finder, although an average per year feature would also be nice”. The Ranked for picker now has Average over the year: every candidate is priced in every month the route flies and sorted by its average week. On a seasonal lane the aeroplane that wins the peak is not always the one that earns the most across twelve months — the big cabin buys its summer with a winter the small cabin never has — and the strip beside each row already showed that; now it can decide the order. Months outside the route’s operating window are left out of the average rather than counted as zero, so a summer-only route is not marked down for flying the schedule you gave it.

The business jets are listed at the foot of the regional jet guide; what a season does to a market is in route economics.
